meta.title: How a solar panel makes electricity
meta.name: Solar, explained
meta.headline: Sunlight knocks electrons loose, and a wire gives them somewhere to go
meta.lede: A silicon solar cell turns about a fifth of the light that hits it into electricity, with no moving parts. Here is the whole trick in four steps.

sections.title: It starts with a sandwich of silicon
sections.body:
A cell is two thin layers of silicon, doped differently so one has spare electrons (**n-type**) and the other is missing some (**p-type**). Where they meet, an electric field forms.

When a photon with enough energy hits the silicon, it frees an electron. The field pushes it one way, and a metal grid collects it.

aside.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  sun([Sunlight]) --> cell[Silicon cell]
  cell -->|frees electrons| field{p-n junction}
  field -->|pushes them out| grid[Metal grid]
  grid --> inv[Inverter]
  inv -->|AC| home[(Your home)]
aside.caption: Light in, direct current out; the inverter turns it into household AC.

sections.title: Four steps from photon to plug

items.title: Absorb
items.body: Silicon absorbs photons with more energy than its band gap (1.1 eV), roughly all visible light.

items.title: Separate
items.body: The junction's field sweeps freed electrons to the n side and holes to the p side.

items.title: Collect
items.body: Thin silver fingers on the front carry the current out without blocking much light.

items.title: Convert
items.body: An inverter changes the panel's DC into AC at your grid's voltage and frequency.

sections.title: What's still hard
sections.body: Storage. Panels make the most at noon; homes use the most in the evening. Batteries close the gap, at a cost.
